items_missed: Additional rooms never probed — no question about a garage, storage closet, patio or balcony at the second-floor apartment, and nothing about which of the three stories at the destination townhome the items are actually going to. She logged 'three story town home' and never asked whether the crew is carrying to floor one, two or three. On a stairs-driven estimate that is the single biggest unknown she left open.

Destination-side access never asked. She asked 'And we can park right in front of the building' about the origin and got a useful answer ('maybe like, fifteen feet'), then asked nothing at all about the townhome end — no parking, no walk, no driveway, no HOA. Half of the labor on this move happens at an address she has zero access detail on.

No 'pricing is super simple' opener. She went in with 'let me walk you through the basics first,' which is functional but drops the simplicity frame that pre-empts the comparison-shopping the customer was about to do.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'This also includes the taxes, insurance, and the gas' is the entire insurance content of the call — no $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no brand name. The customer said her top concern was cost, and $2,000 of included coverage is a value answer she never received.

Clock start never explained. She covered the 2.5-hour minimum and the fifteen-minute proration but never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens — so the customer has no idea whether she is paying for drive time from the branch.

Two different top-end numbers given for the same estimate, seconds apart: 'if we end up using five hour hours that's $970' and then 'again anywhere from $679.07 to $907.' $970 and $907 are not the same number, and the customer is about to forward this to her wife. A $63 swing on a quote that is going to be shopped is a real credibility cost.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors — nothing to make three-and-a-half-to-five hours feel concrete against a 2BR of furniture with no boxes.

Consolidation examples absent from the prep speech. She said 'take the smaller pieces yourself' and stopped — no drawers, no closet odds and ends, no photos off the walls, no garden tools. The generic version is easy to nod at and easy to ignore.
'Take a carload' never said. This is a thirty-minute drive with a customer already hauling all her own boxes — the carload framing was already half-accepted and never got named.

BOLDED-details framing and the 'reply with any corrections' verification ask both absent. She said 'I'll just email you the estimate' and left it there, with no ask for the customer to check the details — on a call where she recapped a long list of addresses, floors and dates that were never read back for confirmation.

No 'any other questions before I let you go?' at the close. She asked 'Do you have any questions? So far about the pricing' mid-block, but the call ended on her own monologue with no final opening for the customer.

Hours never given. 'You know where to call me back or you can just send us an email anytime' is not hours and is not a callback channel — and the decision-maker on this move is a wife who was not on the call.

Customer's name used twice ('I'm looking for Lauren' and 'what are you most worried about for the upcoming move Lauren?') — short of the 3+ standard, and both uses were in question form rather than warmth.
top_strength: Amy runs the cleanest front half of any call in this batch. She is the only rep of the eight to score a full 7/7 on Set The Agenda, and she earned it with a real roadmap rather than a permission ask: 'I'm calling about the quote you requested online. I'd like to ask you some questions first so we can get started on the right track and then I'll build an estimate if you can depend on this call would probably take five to ten minutes. Is this a good time?' That is purpose, sequence, timeframe and confirmation in one breath, and the customer's 'Yeah' was a genuine yes to the structure, not just to talking. She then went straight into a details recap that did real work — date, day-of-week, origin floor, elevator status, both addresses — and the recap caught an error live: she had the apartment as 'a second floor apartment on the third floor' and Lauren corrected her to 'Departments on a third floor,' which Amy immediately locked in with 'Gotcha. Third floor no elevator.' That is the recap bullet earning its points instead of just being said. The second strength is the stressor question, which almost nobody in this batch asks and which she asked by name: 'is there any specific concern or what are you most worried about for the upcoming move Lauren?' It returned the most valuable sentence on the call — 'Probably the cost we're trying to figure out. I don't know if you guys do itemized versus hourly' — and Amy answered the actual question ('we just offer hourly') and then pivoted the entire pricing block to lead with the cheapest-day framing: 'Monday through Thursday, we charge... an hour that is with two movers already.' She sold the day-of-week advantage to a customer whose move was already on a Thursday, which is the right instinct: confirm they're already on the good tier. Third, she did deliver a prep-saves-you-money speech tied to this specific customer's situation — 'when you mentioned earlier that you're going to take all the boxes or if you can also take, or disassemble the bed in advance take the smaller pieces yourself that would help you save time. And of course money by the end of the day does it so fair.' It is abbreviated, but it is real Save Your Ass content, connected to something the customer said herself, and closed with a sense-check. Only two of the eight calls this week contain any version of that speech at all.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Amy built a 7/7 agenda and a good estimate, then gave away the entire differentiator block. No Worries Damage Coverage, Meet Your Mover and On-Time Guarantee are all absent — six points of rubric and, more importantly, the only three things on the call that are not price. Lauren told her outright that cost is the concern and that she is forwarding this to her wife, which means this quote is going into a side-by-side comparison against two or three competitors who also charge roughly $200 an hour. The hourly rate is not the differentiator; the $2,000 coverage, the mover's photo in her inbox, and the discount-if-we're-late promise are. The fix is a fixed thirty-second block that follows the rate every single time: 'And three things that come with every move and cost you nothing extra — No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse anything we damage, which is well past the 60 cents a pound the state requires. A few days out you'll get an email with your movers' photos and names so you know exactly who's knocking. And if we miss your arrival window, we start discounting your bill immediately.' Second priority: the close. She got a warm customer, an email request, and a second decision-maker named out loud ('I need to send the quote to my wife') and never asked for the booking, never offered to hold October 1st, and never asked Lauren to reply and confirm the details. 'October 1st is still wide open, it's just that, you know, calendar may changes' is urgency with no ask attached to it. What she needed: 'There's no deposit and no card on file, so I can hold October 1st for you right now at no cost while you two talk — if you decide differently, just reply and let me know. I'll bold the date, the rate and the estimate at the top of the email so she can read it in ten seconds, and reply with any corrections if I got an address or a floor wrong.' That one move gets the booking attempt, the no-deposit differentiator, the verification ask and the bolded list — four missing bullets in a single paragraph. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: this one is close, but it is worth pulling. She stated the typical 2BR range as 'three and a half to five and a half hours,' said a ground-to-ground version of this job would be 'two and a half to three and a half hours,' then landed at 'three and a half, maybe up to five hours' while narrating her own padding out loud — 'I would suggest this is maybe a bit conservative or super conservative.' Her final range stays inside her stated typical band, so this is not the flagrant version of the pattern, but she said the quiet part into the phone. Two flights of stairs at origin and an unknown number of floors at the destination justify moving up from the ground-to-ground number; saying 'super conservative' to the customer does not add accuracy, it just pre-excuses an overage. And note the deeper problem underneath it: she never asked which floor of the three-story townhome the items are going to, so the stairs variable she is padding for is one she never actually measured. Ask the floor, then quote the range, and drop the word conservative. Last, fix the money. She said '$970' and then '$907' for the same top end within about fifteen seconds, and the rate itself came through as a number that cannot be right. Numbers said once, slowly, and then repeated back — especially on a quote that is being forwarded to a spouse who will only ever see the email.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and energetic word choice throughout — 'Amazing,' 'Okeydokey,' 'Doing well, thank you, thank you for asking,' 'For sure. For sure no worries' — plus the stressor question and two uses of the customer's name, all of which kept the call feeling personal rather than procedural; held back from a 5 by a roughly 150-word uninterrupted pricing block that reduced Lauren to 'Okay. Mm-hmm. Okay.' and by a close that thanked her for her time without ever asking for anything.
audio_review_reason: Two reasons. First, the numbers are unusable as transcribed — the hourly rate comes through as '$19,594 an hour' and the top of the estimate is given as both '$970' and '$907' within seconds. Audio is the only way to know whether Amy actually stated a clean rate and a consistent range to the customer or whether she genuinely fumbled the figures on a quote that was about to be forwarded to a second decision-maker. Second, the score is a 4 on warm transcript language but the customer went nearly monosyllabic for the entire back half ('Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Okay.'), which fits the flagging rule for a 4-or-5 with a disengaged customer — worth hearing whether the pricing block was delivered at a pace Lauren could actually follow.
